props.title: What your venue does to the sound
props.seo_title: What your venue does to the sound: glass, carpet, ceilings and where the speakers go
props.dek: The same band sounds different in a glass atrium and a carpeted ballroom. Here's why, in plain words, the one test you can do yourself in an empty venue, and what to tell the band before they load in.
props.meta_description: Why live music sounds harsh in a glass venue and muddy in a carpeted one, what echo does to speeches, a clap test any planner can do, and why where the speakers point matters more than how big they are.
props.llms_description: A plain-language guide for event planners on how a venue's materials and shape change the sound of a live band: low notes pass through walls (the complaint from the event next door) while the crisp parts of speech and music are absorbed by soft surfaces and by people, so an empty-venue sound check misleads; glass, marble and concrete reflect the high end and feel harsh, carpet and drapes absorb it and leave the low end booming; reverberation (how long sound hangs after it stops) blurs speech, with a clap test to judge it; and speaker placement: aim at people rather than walls, and halving the distance to a listener adds about 6 decibels, so a second small pair of speakers halfway down a long hall covers the back better than a bigger pair at the front. Ends with what to tell the band about the venue.

hero.alt: Long wooden tables set for a wedding under a glass roof, with greenery overhead and light pouring in.

items.text: Glass, marble and concrete throw the crisp part of the sound back at the guests and feel harsh. Carpet and drapes soak it up and leave the low end booming. The band tunes for one or the other.
Echo blurs speech. Clap once in the empty venue: if the sound hangs for more than a second, the toasts need planning.
Where the speakers point matters more than how big they are. Smaller speakers, closer to the tables, aimed at people, beat a big pair at the front.

props.html:
You heard the band at a showcase in a hotel ballroom and they sounded warm and easy. At your venue, a converted warehouse with a glass wall, the same band at the same level sounds sharp, the toasts are hard to follow, and by nine everyone is shouting. The band is the same. The venue is doing the rest.

Here is what a venue does to sound, in plain words, and what to tell the band so they arrive ready for it.

props.text: Two kinds of sound come out of a loudspeaker

props.html:
The first is the low part, the thump of the bass drum and the bass guitar. Those sound waves are long, and long waves pass through walls, roll down a corridor and arrive in the ballroom next door as a thump with no music attached. That thump is the complaint your catering manager gets from the other event.

The second is the crisp part: the consonants in a voice, the snap of a snare drum, the shimmer of a cymbal. Those waves are short, and short waves get soaked up by anything soft, especially people. Two hundred guests in wool and cotton are a wall of absorption that was missing at sound check, which is why a band that sounded fine in an empty ballroom at three can turn muddy at eight.

Glass, marble, tile and polished concrete bounce the crisp part straight back at the guests. Everything feels harsh and tiring at a level that would be comfortable on carpet, and the band turns down to take the edge off, and the bass goes with it.

A carpeted ballroom with drapes does the reverse. The fabric swallows the crisp part, and the low end hangs there with nothing to tame it. The band ends up cutting the bass and brightening everything else.

Both are fine to play in. They are different settings, and the band needs to know which one before the truck is packed, because a glass atrium at cocktail hour often needs no subwoofer at all, and a carpeted ballroom needs a different set of speakers than a glass one.

props.alt: An event space with wood-paneled walls, round tables and pendant lights, set for a dinner.
props.caption: Wood and fabric soak up the crisp part of the sound. Glass throws it back.

props.text: Echo, and a test you can do yourself

props.html:
Every space holds sound for a moment after it stops. In a carpeted ballroom that moment is under a second. In a stone church or a glass atrium it can be two or three seconds. In that long tail, each syllable is still hanging in the air when the next one arrives, and the words blur: fifteen starts to sound like sixteen. A 2025 study of university dining halls found that the less echo a space has, the more of the speech people understand, which matters most during the toasts.

You can measure this without any equipment. Stand in the middle of the empty venue, clap once, hard, and listen. If the sound stops almost at once, the speeches will be easy. If it hangs for a second or more, tell the band. They will bring the speakers closer to the tables and keep the microphone level lower, and the toasts will still land.

The full venue will have less echo than the empty one. A 2020 study found that sound-absorbing panels placed upright near the diners did more for speech than the same panels on the ceiling. Guests are upright absorbers near the diners. The space changes the moment it fills.

The venue's walls are fixed by the time the band arrives. Where the sound starts, and where it points, is up to the band. Speakers aimed across a hall at a glass wall set the whole space ringing. Speakers raised to head height and aimed at people put most of the sound into bodies and clothing, which soak it up.

Distance matters more than size. Halving the distance between a speaker and a listener adds about six decibels for that listener, a clear notch up on the volume knob, without anyone touching it. So in a long hall, a second small pair of speakers halfway back covers the last tables better than a bigger pair at the front ever will, and the first tables don't pay for it.

props.alt: Two top-down diagrams of a long hall with twelve tables. Left, one large pair of speakers at the front: 92 decibels at the first table and 72 at the last. Right, two modest pairs, one at the front and one halfway back: 80 decibels at the first table and 78 at the last.
props.caption: Two ways to cover the same hall. The gap between the first table and the last is the point; the exact levels are illustrative.

props.title: Three things to tell the band about your venue
props.html: What the walls, floor and ceiling are made of, and roughly how high the ceiling is. Whether another event will be running on the other side of a wall. And what the clap test sounded like. A photo from where the band will stand, taken at the time of day the event happens, answers most of it.

We ask about the materials and the ceiling before we quote, and we walk the venue when we can. From that we decide which speakers come, where they point, and whether a subwoofer comes at all. The band loads in knowing whether the space is glass or carpet, and sets up for the full space rather than the empty one.
